[{"role": "user", "content": "Please write a long and detailed answer about why sourdough bread keeps longer than commercial yeast bread."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Sourdough keeps longer chiefly because of what the fermentation does to the dough's chemistry. A sourdough culture is not just yeast; it is a symbiosis of wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria, and those bacteria produce lactic and acetic acid over the long fermentation. The resulting drop in pH creates an environment hostile to the moulds and rope-forming bacteria that spoil bread, so visible spoilage is simply delayed by several days.

The acids also change the starch itself. Staling is not primarily drying out; it is retrogradation, the process by which gelatinized starch molecules recrystallize and force water out of the crumb. The acidic conditions and the longer fermentation partially break down starch and increase the activity of enzymes that interfere with that recrystallization, so the crumb stays soft measurably longer.

Structure contributes too. Long fermentation develops a stronger, more extensible gluten network and produces a thicker, drier crust, which slows moisture migration out of the loaf. Commercial yeast bread, by contrast, is fermented fast, has a near-neutral pH, and often relies on added preservatives or emulsifiers to achieve a shelf life that sourdough gets from its own biology."}]

Simple interest pays out on the principal alone, so it grows in a straight line. Compounding folds each payment back into the balance, so the base on which interest is calculated keeps expanding, and growth curves upward.

The mechanics depend on the compounding frequency. If a balance compounds annually, interest is added once a year. If it compounds monthly, one twelfth of the annual rate is applied twelve times, and each application works on a slightly larger balance than the last. More frequent compounding therefore yields slightly more over the same period at the same nominal rate.

A worked example makes this concrete. Put $10,000 into an account paying 6% compounded annually. After year one you have $10,600. The mechanics depend on the compounding frequency. If a balance compounds annually, interest is added once a year. The most useful reviews are prompt and small.
